fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Balaam asks for seven altars (Numbers 23:1), and the text says “…Balak did as Balaam had instructed…” (Numbers 23:2). No argument is recorded anywhere. Seven altars is a big order, and I think most of us would grumble a little, but Balak just starts building.

Right, and here's what the text says. Balaam asks for seven altars, seven bulls and seven rams (Numbers 23:1), and Balak does as he's told (Numbers 23:2). The text records no pushback at all. I'd have wanted at least one question about that order, probably two.

The whole land of Canaan isn't what the text gives. It says Balaam “…could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.” (Numbers 22:41). Just the edges of the camp, nothing more. It's like peeking through a bakery keyhole and getting only the doormat.

Carmel isn't named in this passage. The text says Balak took Balaam “…to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah…” (Numbers 23:14). The king keeps changing the scenery, like a man rearranging the furniture and hoping the room will say something different. Pisgah is the mountain this passage names.

True. Balak says, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (Numbers 23:25). Earlier he asked for a curse (Numbers 23:13), so this is a big change. I think two blessings in a row changed his order.

Balak's words are, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). His hope is about a curse from a new place, not about the camp. Nothing in the text has Israel moving anywhere. It's like switching lanes in traffic and hoping the jam ends in the new one.
The text says Peor “…overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). Third mountain, third try, and the view is a wasteland. I think Balak is running low on scenic options. Wasteland is the word to keep.
